The replica-symmetric free energy for Ising spin glasses with orthogonally invariant couplingsThanks: Z. Fan is supported in part by NSF Grants DMS-1916198 and DMS-2142476. Y. Wu is supported in part by NSF Grant CCF-1900507, an NSF CAREER award CCF-1651588, and an Alfred Sloan fellowship.

Zhou Fan Email address: zhou.fan@yale.edu (corresponding) and Yihong Wu Address: Department of Statistics and Data Science
Yale University
New Haven
CT
USA Email address: yihong.wu@yale.edu
Abstract.

We study a variant of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (S-K) spin glass model with external field, where the random symmetric couplings matrix does not consist of i.i.d. entries but is instead orthogonally invariant in law. For sufficiently high temperature, we prove a replica-symmetric formula for the first-order limit of the model free energy. Our analysis is an adaptation of a conditional second-moment-method argument previously introduced by Bolthausen for studying the high-temperature regime of the S-K model, where one conditions on the iterates of an Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithm for solving the TAP equations for the model magnetization. We apply this method using a memory-free version of AMP that is tailored to the orthogonally invariant structure of the model couplings.

1. Introduction

We study a probability model on the hypercube σ∈{+1,−1}n\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n} given by

(1.1) P⁡(σ)=1Z​exp⁡(β2​σ⊤​J​σ+h⊤​σ).P(\sigma)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{\top}J\sigma+h^{\top}\sigma\right).

Here h∈ℝnh\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is a deterministic vector, J∈ℝn×nJ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a random symmetric matrix which we will assume satisfies the orthogonal invariance in law

J​=𝐿​O⊤​J​O​ for any orthogonal matrix ​O∈ℝn×n,J\overset{L}{=}O^{\top}JO\text{ for any orthogonal matrix }O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},

and ZZ is the partition function

Z=∑σ∈{+1,−1}nexp⁡(β2​σ⊤​J​σ+h⊤​σ).Z=\sum_{\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n}}\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{\top}J\sigma+h^{\top}\sigma\right).

We will refer to JJ as the couplings matrix, hh as the external field, and β\beta as the inverse temperature.

The specific example of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (S-K) model [49], where JJ has i.i.d. Gaussian entries above the diagonal, is well-studied and known to exhibit rich phenomena. At high temperatures, P⁡(σ)P(\sigma) is “replica-symmetric”, the large-nn limit of the free energy is described by a simple replica-symmetric formula [49, 1, 8], and the magnetization m=∑σ∈{+1,−1}nσ⋅P⁡(σ)m=\sum_{\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n}}\sigma\cdot P(\sigma) satisfies in this limit the Thouless-Anderson-Palmer (TAP) mean-field equations [56, 13, 55]. At low temperatures, the limit free energy is described more generally by Parisi’s variational formula [43, 44, 25, 54]. The solution of the variational problem may be understood as corresponding to an ultrametric tree structure for P⁡(σ)P(\sigma), and the TAP equations describe the conditional means of the “pure states” in this ultrametric tree [35, 36, 37]. This picture has been formalized and proven rigorously for certain mixed pp-spin analogues of the S-K model in [42, 3].

Here, we are interested in the more general setting of (1.1) where JJ is orthogonally invariant, but can have arbitrary spectral distribution and dependent entries. Examples include the random orthogonal model (ROM) [34] where JJ has all eigenvalues equal to {+1,−1}\{+1,-1\}, and the Gaussian Hopfield model [27] where J=G⊤​GJ=G^{\top}G and GG is a rectangular Gaussian matrix. In the physics literature, the replica-symmetric and 1-RSB free energies for the ROM were computed by Marinari et al. in [34], and extended to models with general orthogonally invariant couplings in [14]. Parisi and Potters derived in [45] the TAP mean-field equations for the ROM, using a perturbative expansion approach of [46, 23] and a conjectured resummation of the terms of this expansion. Opper and Winther provided in [41] an alternative derivation of the TAP equations using the cavity method and a system of self-consistent equations for the cavity fields (which we review in Appendix E), and verified also via a replica calculation that the TAP free energy evaluated at the model magnetization coincides with the free energy given by the replica-symmetric formula. At present, few rigorous mathematical results are known for models with general orthogonally invariant couplings matrices JJ.

Our work is in large part motivated by a renewed interest in these types of mean-field models in information theory, statistics, and machine learning [50, 57, 48, 51, 31, 4, 47, 18, 21, 24, 30, 33, 53, 52], where orthogonally invariant matrices may serve as more robust models of regression and sensing designs or more accurate models of noise in data applications. Indeed, following the initial posting of this work, several dynamical universality results were obtained in [19, 58, 20] showing that the mean-field dynamics of Approximate Message Passing (AMP) and other first-order iterative algorithms applied to orthogonally invariant matrices are universal across broad classes of matrices with delocalized eigenvectors. In many of these applications, replica predictions for the model free energy are conjectured, but not rigorously known. Maillard et al. studied in [32] a class of computational algorithms in the context of such orthogonally invariant models, extending the diagrammatic expansion method of [46, 23, 45] to describe the connections between these algorithms and the predicted mean field theory; the authors of [32] highlighted the mathematical verification of these predictions as an open question.

We study in this work the specific model (1.1), and prove a replica-symmetric formula for the first-order limit of its free energy in a sufficiently high temperature regime. This extends previous work of [6], which showed such a result in the absence of an external field (h=0h=0). Similar to the S-K model [1], the h=0h=0 setting is special in that the quenched free energy n−1​𝔼​log⁡Zn^{-1}\mathbb{E}\log Z coincides asymptotically with the annealed free energy n−1​log⁡𝔼​Zn^{-1}\log\mathbb{E}Z, as was verified in [6] using the second moment method. This no longer holds when h≠0h\neq 0, and our proof applies instead a conditional version of this idea developed in [8] for the S-K model, where one establishes that the quenched and annealed free energies coincide upon conditioning on an appropriately chosen sigma-field that is informative about the random magnetization. This method was refined for the S-K model in [11] to cover a large and explicit part of the high-temperature regime, and is also related to analyses of [16, 9] for the Ising perceptron model.

Our construction of the conditioning sigma-field relies on recent developments on iterative algorithms for solving the TAP equations for the model (1.1). We summarize these developments and the proof strategy in Section 1.2 below, after presenting our main result. Following the initial posting of this work, our analyses have been extended in [22] to show also the validity of the TAP equations for the magnetization under a similar high-temperature assumption, and in [29] to obtain analogous results in a statistical linear model with orthogonally invariant regression design.

1.1. Model and main result

Consider the Gibbs distribution (1.1) on the binary hypercube, under the following assumptions for the couplings matrix JJ and external field hh.

    limn→∞max(d1,…,dn)=d+≜max(x:x∈supp(μD)),lim infn→∞min(d1,…,dn)>−∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\max(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n})=d_{+}\triangleq\max(x:x\in\supp(\mu_{D})),\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}\min(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n})>-\infty.

    1n​∑i=1nδhi→μH\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{h_{i}}\to\mu_{H}

    as n→∞n\to\infty. For every p≥1p\geq 1, the law μH\mu_{H} has finite pthp^{\text{th}} moment, and n−1​∑i=1nhip→𝔼𝖧∼μH​[𝖧p]n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{i}^{p}\to\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{H}\sim\mu_{H}}[\mathsf{H}^{p}].11 1 This moment condition for hh is used to apply the AMP state evolution analysis of [21] to deduce Theorem 2.2, and is not used in the rest of the argument.

We are interested in the asymptotic free energy

G⁡(z)=∫1z−x​μD​(𝑑x),R⁡(z)=G−1​(z)−1z.G(z)=\int\frac{1}{z-x}\mu_{D}(dx),\qquad R(z)=G^{-1}(z)-\frac{1}{z}.

Theorem 1.3.

Suppose Assumption 1.1 holds. Then for some β0=β0​(μD)>0\beta_{0}=\beta_{0}(\mu_{D})>0 depending only on μD\mu_{D}, and for any fixed β∈(0,β0)\beta\in(0,\beta_{0}), almost surely

limn→∞1n​log⁡Z=ΨRS.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log Z=\Psi_{\mathrm{RS}}.

We mention that for the spherical counterpart of the Ising model (1.1), the free energy can be computed directly and also agrees with its replica-symmetric prediction. We carry out this computation in Appendix D by applying one of the technical results in Section 2.4.

1.2. Overview of the proof

We will adopt the conditional second moment method of [8], and show that

(1.5) limn→∞1n​log⁡𝔼⁡[Z∣𝒢]≈ΨR​S,limn→∞1n​log⁡𝔼⁡[Z2∣𝒢]≈2​ΨR​S\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{G}]\approx\Psi_{RS},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}]\approx 2\Psi_{RS}

for an appropriately chosen sigma-field 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Together with classical concentration-of-measure results for Haar measure over the orthogonal group, this will be enough to show Theorem 1.3.

We define 𝒢=𝒢t\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}_{t} as the sigma-field generated by a fixed number tt of iterations of an AMP algorithm designed to solve the TAP mean-field equations described in [45, 41]—see (2.11) below. Such an algorithm was introduced for the S-K model in [7] and for applications in compressed sensing in [17, 5]. For the Ising model (1.1) with orthogonally invariant couplings, a general class of AMP-type procedures was described in [40], including a “single-step memory” algorithm for solving the TAP equations that reduces to the one of [7] in the S-K setting. Our analyses will rely on a rigorous characterization of the state evolution of such algorithms obtained in [21].

The specific algorithm we use to construct 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} is not of the single-step memory form of [7, 40], but rather an alternative “memory-free” form introduced by Çakmak and Opper in [12], applying the general procedure in [40] with a resolvent of JJ instead of the couplings matrix JJ itself. This memory-free algorithm is related to a class of Vector/Orthogonal AMP algorithms developed for compressed sensing applications in [31, 51, 47], and may be derived also from the Expectation Propagation framework of Minka [38]. For our purposes, use of this algorithm leads to two important simplifications: First, its state evolution has a simple description when JJ is non-Gaussian, whereas that of alternative iterative procedures may have a complicated dependence on the spectral free cumulants of JJ. Second, the analysis of [21] reveals that iterates of this algorithm have an asymptotic freeness property with respect to JJ, which we describe below in Proposition 2.4. Both simplifications are important in enabling our computations of the conditional moments in (1.5).

The details of our strategy for showing (1.5) are somewhat different from those presented in [8], and we proceed in two high-level steps: We first apply the AMP state evolution and a large deviations argument to give exact expressions for the large-nn limits of the conditional moments (1.5) in terms of low-dimensional variational problems. This leverages and extends some results of Guionnet and Maıda [26] that relate exponential integrals over the orthogonal group to the R-transform of JJ. We then analyze these variational problems, proving upper and lower bounds for their values that are tight for ΨRS\Psi_{\mathrm{RS}} and 2​ΨRS2\Psi_{\mathrm{RS}} in the limit as the number of algorithm iterations t→∞t\to\infty. The assumption of small β\beta (i.e. sufficiently high temperature) is used in a crucial way in the upper bounds, to show a global concavity property of these variational problems.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we collect the general ingredients of the proof, including a more detailed description of the AMP algorithm and its state evolution, and the evaluations of the required exponential integrals over the orthogonal group. In Sections 3 and 4, we analyze the conditional first moment 𝔼⁡[Z∣𝒢t]\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}] and second moment 𝔼⁡[Z2∣𝒢t]\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}] respectively, leading to the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Section 5.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Centering and rescaling

Adding a multiple of the identity to JJ shifts the free energy Ψ\Psi and ΨRS\Psi_{\mathrm{RS}} by the same additive constant. Thus, we may assume without loss of generality that

(2.1) ∫x​μD​(𝑑x)=0.\int x\,\mu_{D}(dx)=0.

Since μD\mu_{D} has positive variance by Assumption 1.1(b), we may also assume without loss of generality that

(2.2) ∫x2​μD​(𝑑x)=1,\int x^{2}\,\mu_{D}(dx)=1,

by rescaling J=O⊤​D​OJ=O^{\top}DO and incorporating this scaling into β\beta.

For most of the proof, it will be notationally convenient to absorb the parameter β\beta into the couplings matrix JJ, after this centering and rescaling. We define

(2.3) J¯=β​J,D¯=diag⁡(d¯1,…,d¯n)=β​D,μD¯=limn→∞1n​∑i=1nδdi¯,d¯+=β​d+.\bar{J}=\beta J,\qquad\bar{D}=\diag(\bar{d}_{1},\ldots,\bar{d}_{n})=\beta D,\qquad\mu_{\bar{D}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\bar{d_{i}}},\qquad\bar{d}_{+}=\beta d_{+}.

Thus μD¯\mu_{\bar{D}} is the rescaling of the limit spectral law μD\mu_{D}, and d¯+=max(x:x∈supp(μD¯))\bar{d}_{+}=\max(x:x\in\supp(\mu_{\bar{D}})) is its maximum point of support.

We denote the Cauchy- and R-transforms of μD¯\mu_{\bar{D}} by

where G¯​(z)\bar{G}(z) is defined on (d¯+,∞)(\bar{d}_{+},\infty), and R¯​(z)\bar{R}(z) on (0,G¯​(d¯+))(0,\bar{G}(\bar{d}_{+})). These are related to the Cauchy- and R-transforms of μD\mu_{D} by

(2.5) G¯​(z)=1β​G​(zβ),R¯​(z)=β​R​(β​z).\bar{G}(z)=\frac{1}{\beta}G\left(\frac{z}{\beta}\right),\qquad\bar{R}(z)=\beta R(\beta z).

2.2. AMP for solving the TAP equations

Denote by

m=∑σ∈{+1,−1}nσ⋅P⁡(σ)∈(−1,1)nm=\sum_{\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n}}\sigma\cdot P(\sigma)\in(-1,1)^{n}

(2.11) m=tanh⁡(h+J¯​m−R¯​(1−q∗)​m).m=\tanh\Big(h+\bar{J}m-\bar{R}(1-q_{*})m\Big).

(2.12) λ∗=G¯−1​(1−q∗)=R¯​(1−q∗)+11−q∗\lambda_{*}=\bar{G}^{-1}(1-q_{*})=\bar{R}(1-q_{*})+\frac{1}{1-q_{*}}

(2.13) Γ=O⊤​Λ​O,Λ=11−q∗​(λ∗​I−D¯)−1−I.\Gamma=O^{\top}\Lambda O,\qquad\Lambda=\frac{1}{1-q_{*}}(\lambda_{*}I-\bar{D})^{-1}-I.

In particular, Γ\Gamma is also orthogonally invariant in law. Let y0∈ℝny^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be an initialization of the AMP algorithm with entries

(2.14) y10,…,yn0​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,σ∗2),y_{1}^{0},\ldots,y_{n}^{0}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{*}^{2}),

where σ∗2\sigma_{*}^{2} is defined in (2.9). Then the AMP algorithm is given by the iterations

3. Conditional first moment

Let ZZ be the partition function in (2.8), and let 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} be the sigma-field defined by (2.20). We show in this section the following result.

Lemma 3.1.

In the setting of Theorem 1.3,

limt→∞limn→∞1n​log⁡𝔼⁡[Z∣𝒢t]=ΨRS,\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}]=\Psi_{\mathrm{RS}},

where the inner limit as n→∞n\to\infty exists almost surely for each fixed tt.

3.1. Derivation of the variational formula

For scalar arguments γ>d¯+\gamma>\bar{d}_{+} and u,U∈ℝu,U\in\mathbb{R}, and vector arguments v,w,V,W∈ℝtv,w,V,W\in\mathbb{R}^{t} with ‖v‖2+‖w‖2<1\|v\|^{2}+\|w\|^{2}<1, we define the function

Lemma 4.5.

For a constant β0=β0​(μD)>0\beta_{0}=\beta_{0}(\mu_{D})>0 and any β∈(0,β0)\beta\in(0,\beta_{0}),

ℓ~∗\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{*} =ℓ∗+(1−q∗)[Δt−1/2δt−Δt1/2et]=ℓ∗+ot(1)\displaystyle=\ell_{*}+(1-q_{*})[\Delta_{t}^{-1/2}\delta_{t}-\Delta_{t}^{1/2}e_{t}]=\ell_{*}+o_{t}(1)

and δt=(δ1,t+1,…,δt,t+1)\delta_{t}=(\delta_{1,t+1},\ldots,\delta_{t,t+1}) is as defined in the proof of Lemma 3.5. Note that

5. Proof of Theorem 1.3

Finally, using Lemmas 3.1 and 4.1, we conclude the proof of Theorem 1.3.

Proof.

We first show concentration of n−1​log⁡Zn^{-1}\log Z around its mean: Writing σ⊤​J​σ=Tr⁡σ​σ⊤​O⊤​D​O\sigma^{\top}J\sigma=\Tr\sigma\sigma^{\top}O^{\top}DO and viewing Z=Z⁡(O)Z=Z(O) as a function of O∈ℝn×nO\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, we have

∂Olog⁡Z⁡(O)=1Z​∑σ∈{+1,−1}nβ​σ​σ⊤​O⊤​D⋅exp⁡(β2​σ⊤​J​σ+h⊤​σ).\partial_{O}\log Z(O)=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n}}\beta\sigma\sigma^{\top}O^{\top}D\cdot\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{\top}J\sigma+h^{\top}\sigma\right).

Then the Frobenius norm of this derivative (for any O∈ℝn×nO\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}) is bounded as

‖∂Olog⁡Z⁡(O)‖F≤maxσ∈{+1,−1}n⁡‖β​σ​σ⊤​O⊤​D‖F=n​β2⋅σ⊤​O⊤​D2​O​σ≤n​β​‖D‖op​‖O‖op.\|\partial_{O}\log Z(O)\|_{\rm F}\leq\max_{\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}^{n}}\|\beta\sigma\sigma^{\top}O^{\top}D\|_{\rm F}=\sqrt{n\beta^{2}\cdot\sigma^{\top}O^{\top}D^{2}O\sigma}\leq n\beta\|D\|_{\rm op}\|O\|_{\rm op}.

So for any O,O′∈𝕆⁡(n)O,O^{\prime}\in\mathbb{O}(n), integrating along a linear path from OO to O′O^{\prime} in ℝn×n\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},

|log⁡Z⁡(O)−log⁡Z⁡(O′)|≤‖O−O′‖F⋅n​β​‖D‖op.|\log Z(O)-\log Z(O^{\prime})|\leq\|O-O^{\prime}\|_{F}\cdot n\beta\|D\|_{\rm op}.

We apply Gromov’s concentration inequality in the form of [2, Corollary 4.4.28]: Let Q∼𝕊​𝕆​(n)Q\sim\mathbb{SO}(n) and O∼𝕆⁡(n)O\sim\mathbb{O}(n) be independent. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

(5.1) ℙ[|1nlogZ(O)−1n𝔼[logZ(OQ)∣O]|>ε]≤2exp(−(n4−12)​ε22​β2​‖D‖op2).\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\frac{1}{n}\log Z(O)-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\log Z(OQ)\mid O]\right|>\varepsilon\right]\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\left(\frac{n}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\varepsilon^{2}}{2\beta^{2}\|D\|_{\rm op}^{2}}\right).

For any diagonal sign matrix PP with diagonal entries {+1,−1}\{+1,-1\}, note that O⊤​D​O=O⊤​P⊤​D​P​OO^{\top}DO=O^{\top}P^{\top}DPO, so that Z⁡(O)=Z⁡(P​O)Z(O)=Z(PO). Then for any fixed O∈𝕆⁡(n)O\in\mathbb{O}(n), the conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[log⁡Z⁡(O​Q)∣O]\mathbb{E}[\log Z(OQ)\mid O] over Q∼Haar⁡(𝕊​𝕆​(n))Q\sim\Haar(\mathbb{SO}(n)) coincides with that over Q∼Haar⁡(𝕆⁡(n))Q\sim\Haar(\mathbb{O}(n)), which in turn equals the unconditional expectation 𝔼⁡[log⁡Z⁡(O)]\mathbb{E}[\log Z(O)] over O∼Haar⁡(𝕆⁡(n))O\sim\Haar(\mathbb{O}(n)) by the invariance of the Haar measure. Thus under Assumption 1.1(b), for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and a constant c=c⁡(ε,β,μD)>0c=c(\varepsilon,\beta,\mu_{D})>0,

(5.2) ℙ[|1nlogZ−1n𝔼logZ|≤ε]≥1−e−c​n.\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\frac{1}{n}\log Z-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\log Z\right|\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 1-e^{-cn}.

The remainder of the argument is the same as in [8], but for convenience we reproduce it here. Fix any ε>0\varepsilon>0. First observe that by Lemma 3.1, for a large enough iteration t=t⁡(ε)t=t(\varepsilon), almost surely

Proposition C.1.

Let S,TS,T be two fixed metric spaces. For each n≥1n\geq 1, let KnK_{n} be a compact metric space, fn:Kn→Sf_{n}:K_{n}\to S a continuous map, and vn:Kn→Tv_{n}:K_{n}\to T a map that is both continuous and relatively open.55 5 That is, vn​(Un)v_{n}(U_{n}) is open in vn​(Kn)v_{n}(K_{n}) for any open subset Un⊂KnU_{n}\subset K_{n}. For each n≥1n\geq 1, let UnU_{n} be a dense subset of KnK_{n} such that

    For some fixed subset V⊂TV\subset T, we have vn​(Un)=Vv_{n}(U_{n})=V for every nn, and

  • •

    There exists a function f:V→Sf:V\to S such that fn​(x)−f⁡(vn​(x))→0f_{n}(x)-f(v_{n}(x))\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty, uniformly over x∈Unx\in U_{n}.

Then vn​(Kn)=V¯v_{n}(K_{n})=\bar{V} (the closure of VV in TT) for every nn, this function ff is continuous on VV and extends continuously to V¯\bar{V}, and fn​(x)−f⁡(vn​(x))→0f_{n}(x)-f(v_{n}(x))\to 0 uniformly also over x∈Knx\in K_{n}.

For x∈Knx\in K_{n} and v∈Tv\in T, denote Bη​(x)={x′∈Kn:‖x−x′‖<η}B_{\eta}(x)=\{x^{\prime}\in K_{n}:\|x-x^{\prime}\|<\eta\} and Bδ​(v)={v′∈T:‖v−v′‖<δ}B_{\delta}(v)=\{v^{\prime}\in T:\|v-v^{\prime}\|<\delta\}. Then

Proposition C.2.

Let D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a convex set and f:D→ℝf:D\to\mathbb{R} be convex and twice differentiable. Given x∗∈Dx_{*}\in D such that B⁡(x∗,δ)={x:‖x−x∗‖<δ}⊂DB(x_{*},\delta)=\{x:\|x-x_{*}\|<\delta\}\subset D, suppose ‖∇f​(x∗)‖≤ε\|\nabla f(x_{*})\|\leq\varepsilon and ∇2f​(x)⪰c​I\nabla^{2}f(x)\succeq cI for all x∈B⁡(x∗,δ)x\in B(x_{*},\delta), where c​δ>4​εc\delta>4\varepsilon. Then

infx∈Df⁡(x)≥f⁡(x∗)−4​ε2c.\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\geq f(x_{*})-\frac{4\varepsilon^{2}}{c}.

For each x∈B⁡(x∗,δ)x\in B(x_{*},\delta), we have f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x∗)+(∇f​(x∗))⊤​(x−x∗)+c2​‖x−x∗‖2f(x)\geq f(x_{*})+(\nabla f(x_{*}))^{\top}(x-x_{*})+\frac{c}{2}\|x-x_{*}\|^{2}. By convexity of ff, x~\tilde{x} is also the global minimizer so infx∈Df⁡(x)=f⁡(x~)\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=f(\tilde{x}). Finally, f⁡(x~)≥f⁡(x∗)+(∇f​(x∗))⊤​(x−x∗)≥f⁡(x∗)−4​ε2/cf(\tilde{x})\geq f(x_{*})+(\nabla f(x_{*}))^{\top}(x-x_{*})\geq f(x_{*})-4\varepsilon^{2}/c. ∎

(D.5) 𝔼⁡[f⁡(J¯,γ)]=γ+‖h‖2n2​∑i=1n1γ−d¯i−1n​log​det(γ​I−D¯)−1→n→∞Ψ⁡(γ).\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{J},\gamma)]=\gamma+\frac{\|h\|^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\gamma-\bar{d}_{i}}-\frac{1}{n}\log\det(\gamma I-\bar{D})-1\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\Psi(\gamma).

Next we argue that f⁡(J¯,γ)f(\bar{J},\gamma) concentrates, similar to the proof of Theorem 1.3. Viewing f⁡(J¯,γ)f(\bar{J},\gamma) as a function of OO via (D.2), we may compute its derivative

∂Of⁡(J¯,γ)=2n​h​h⊤​O⊤​(γ​I−D¯)−1.\partial_{O}f(\bar{J},\gamma)=\frac{2}{n}hh^{\top}O^{\top}(\gamma I-\bar{D})^{-1}.

Thus for large enough nn and any γ≥d++ε\gamma\geq d_{+}+\varepsilon, we have ‖∂Of⁡(J¯,γ)‖F≤4​‖h‖2n​ε​‖O‖op\|\partial_{O}f(\bar{J},\gamma)\|_{\rm F}\leq\frac{4\|h\|^{2}}{n\varepsilon}\|O\|_{\rm op}. By Assumption 1.1(c), for all sufficiently large nn, 1n​‖h‖2≤2​𝔼​[𝖧2]\frac{1}{n}\|h\|^{2}\leq 2\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{H}^{2}] and hence O↦f⁡(J¯,γ)O\mapsto f(\bar{J},\gamma) is LL-Lipschitz on 𝕆⁡(n)\mathbb{O}(n) with L=8​𝔼​[𝖧2]εL=\frac{8\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{H}^{2}]}{\varepsilon}. Then by the same argument that leads to (5.1) and (5.2), we have for each γ≥d¯++ε\gamma\geq\bar{d}_{+}+\varepsilon,

(D.6) ℙ[|f(J¯,γ)−𝔼[f(J¯,γ)]|≥δ]≤2exp{−(n4−12)​δ22​L2}.\mathbb{P}\left[|f(\bar{J},\gamma)-\mathbb{E}[f(\bar{J},\gamma)]|\geq\delta\right]\leq 2\exp\left\{-\frac{(\frac{n}{4}-\frac{1}{2})\delta^{2}}{2L^{2}}\right\}.

Furthermore, |∂γf⁡(J¯,γ)|≤1+‖h‖2n​ε+1ε|\partial_{\gamma}f(\bar{J},\gamma)|\leq 1+\frac{\|h\|^{2}}{n\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}. Thus for all O∈𝕆⁡(n)O\in\mathbb{O}(n) and all sufficiently large nn, γ↦f⁡(J¯,γ)\gamma\mapsto f(\bar{J},\gamma) is L′L^{\prime}-Lipschitz with L′=1+(2​𝔼​[𝖧2]+1)/εL^{\prime}=1+(2\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{H}^{2}]+1)/\varepsilon on [d¯++ε,Γ][\bar{d}_{+}+\varepsilon,\Gamma]. The same Lipschitz continuity holds for Ψ⁡(γ)\Psi(\gamma). Combining (D.5) and (D.6), and applying Borel-Cantelli and a union bound over a sufficiently fine grid of values γ∈[d¯++ε,Γ]\gamma\in[\bar{d}_{+}+\varepsilon,\Gamma], we obtain the almost-sure convergence f⁡(J¯,γ)→Ψ⁡(γ)f(\bar{J},\gamma)\to\Psi(\gamma) uniformly over γ∈[d¯++ε,Γ]\gamma\in[\bar{d}_{+}+\varepsilon,\Gamma]. Then by (D.3) and (D.4), also f⁡(J¯)→ΨRS,spheref(\bar{J})\to\Psi_{\mathrm{RS},\mathrm{sphere}}, completing the proof. ∎

Appendix E Cavity-method derivation of the TAP equations

We provide a brief review of the heuristic approach in [41] for deriving the TAP equations (2.11). Let

(E.1) mi=⟨σi⟩,χi​j=⟨σi​σj⟩−⟨σi⟩​⟨σj⟩m_{i}=\langle\sigma_{i}\rangle,\qquad\chi_{ij}=\langle\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}\rangle-\langle\sigma_{i}\rangle\langle\sigma_{j}\rangle

where ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle is the expectation under the law P⁡(σ)P(\sigma) in our model of interest (2.8). Define the cavity field θi=∑j≠iJ¯i​j​σj\theta_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{J}_{ij}\sigma_{j}. Then the single-spin marginals of P⁡(σ)P(\sigma) are

P⁡(σi)=1Zi​⟨eσi​(hi+θi)⟩∖i,Zi=∑σi∈{±1}⟨eσi​(hi+θi)⟩∖iP(\sigma_{i})=\frac{1}{Z_{i}}\langle e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\theta_{i})}\rangle_{\setminus i},\qquad Z_{i}=\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}}\langle e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\theta_{i})}\rangle_{\setminus i}

where ⟨⋅⟩∖i\langle\cdot\rangle_{\setminus i} denotes the expectation over {σj}j≠i\{\sigma_{j}\}_{j\neq i} (defining θi\theta_{i}) in the cavity system with the spin σi\sigma_{i} removed. We have the exact identities

(E.2) mi=∂hilog⁡Zi,χi​j=∂hjmi.m_{i}=\partial_{h_{i}}\log Z_{i},\qquad\chi_{ij}=\partial_{h_{j}}m_{i}.

Approximating the law of the cavity field θi\theta_{i} under ⟨⋅⟩∖i\langle\cdot\rangle_{\setminus i} by a Gaussian law 𝒩⁡(μi,vi)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},v_{i}), one obtains from the Gaussian moment-generating-function

(E.3) P⁡(σi)≈1Zi​eσi​(hi+μi)+vi/2,mi≈tanh⁡(hi+μi),Zi≈∑σi∈{±1}eσi​(hi+μi)+vi/2.P(\sigma_{i})\approx\frac{1}{Z_{i}}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\mu_{i})+v_{i}/2},\qquad m_{i}\approx\tanh(h_{i}+\mu_{i}),\qquad Z_{i}\approx\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\mu_{i})+v_{i}/2}.

Furthermore, the law of θi\theta_{i} under ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle in the original model is then approximately a two-component Gaussian mixture P(θi)∝∑σi∈{±1}eσi​(hi+θi)−(θi−μi)2/2​vi∝∑σi∈{±1}eσi​(hi+μi)e−(θi−μi−σivi)2/2viP(\theta_{i})\propto\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\theta_{i})-(\theta_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2}/2v_{i}}\propto\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\mu_{i})}e^{-(\theta_{i}-\mu_{i}-\sigma_{i}v_{i})^{2}/2v_{i}}, from which one obtains ⟨θi⟩≈μi+vi​tanh⁡(hi+μi)≈μi+vi​mi\langle\theta_{i}\rangle\approx\mu_{i}+v_{i}\tanh(h_{i}+\mu_{i})\approx\mu_{i}+v_{i}m_{i}. Equating this with ⟨θi⟩=∑k≠iJ¯i​k​mk\langle\theta_{i}\rangle=\sum_{k\neq i}\bar{J}_{ik}m_{k} from the definition of θi\theta_{i} gives

(E.4) μi≈∑kJ¯i​k​mk−vi​mi.\mu_{i}\approx\sum_{k}\bar{J}_{ik}m_{k}-v_{i}m_{i}.

Finally, the approach of [41] is to derive an equation for the cavity field variances {vi}\{v_{i}\} by implicit differentiation in hjh_{j}, assuming ∂hjvi≈0\partial_{h_{j}}v_{i}\approx 0. Then, differentiating (E.4) and applying (E.2),

(E.5) ∂hjμi≈∑kJ¯i​k​χk​j−vi​χi​j.\partial_{h_{j}}\mu_{i}\approx\sum_{k}\bar{J}_{ik}\chi_{kj}-v_{i}\chi_{ij}.

Differentiating the first equality of (E.2) using the approximation for ZiZ_{i} in (E.3),

(E.6) χi​j=∂hjmi≈∂hj∑σiσi​eσi​(hi+μi)+vi/2∑σieσi​(hi+μi)+vi/2≈χi​i(𝟏{i=j}+∂hjμi).\chi_{ij}=\partial_{h_{j}}m_{i}\approx\partial_{h_{j}}\frac{\sum_{\sigma_{i}}\sigma_{i}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\mu_{i})+v_{i}/2}}{\sum_{\sigma_{i}}e^{\sigma_{i}(h_{i}+\mu_{i})+v_{i}/2}}\approx\chi_{ii}\Big(\mathbf{1}\{i=j\}+\partial_{h_{j}}\mu_{i}\Big).

Combining (E.5) and (E.6), and denoting χ=(χi​j)i,j=1N\chi=(\chi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{N}, X=diag⁡(χi​i)i=1NX=\diag(\chi_{ii})_{i=1}^{N}, and V=diag⁡(vi)i=1NV=\diag(v_{i})_{i=1}^{N}, one obtains χ≈X⁡(I+J¯​χ−V​χ)\chi\approx X(I+\bar{J}\chi-V\chi), hence χ≈(V+X−1−J¯)−1\chi\approx(V+X^{-1}-\bar{J})^{-1}. Taking the trace and assuming further by the symmetries of the model that χi​i≈1−q∗\chi_{ii}\approx 1-q_{*} and vi≈vv_{i}\approx v for some v>0v>0 and all i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N, this gives 1−q∗≈G¯​(v+11−q∗)1-q_{*}\approx\bar{G}(v+\frac{1}{1-q_{*}}), i.e. v≈R¯​(1−q∗)v\approx\bar{R}(1-q_{*}), where 1N​Tr⁡(z​I−J¯)→G¯​(z)\frac{1}{N}\Tr(zI-\bar{J})\to\bar{G}(z) as N→∞N\to\infty and G¯,R¯\bar{G},\bar{R} are the Cauchy and R transforms of the limiting law μ¯D¯\bar{\mu}_{\bar{D}} defined in (2.4). Substituting this into (E.3–E.4) yields m≈tanh⁡(h+μ)≈tanh⁡(h+J¯​m−R¯​(1−q∗)​m)m\approx\tanh(h+\mu)\approx\tanh(h+\bar{J}m-\bar{R}(1-q_{*})m) which are the TAP equations (2.11).
